cemc-fryer-2025-01b.title: Subtract the known days
cemc-fryer-2025-01b.body:
The known days total $7 + 15 + 23 = 45$, leaving $73 - 45 = 28$ for Wednesday and Friday together. They are equal, so each is 14.

**Answer: $x = 14$**

cemc-fryer-2025-01c.title: Use the middle day
cemc-fryer-2025-01c.body:
The five numbers go up by equal steps, so their average is Wednesday's number: $100 \div 5 = 20$. Monday is two steps earlier: $20 - 12 = 8$.

**Answer: $y = 8$**

cemc-fryer-2025-02a.title: Points per game
cemc-fryer-2025-02a.body:
Each tie gives out 2 points and each decided game gives out $W = 3$. Two ties and one decided game: $S = 2 + 2 + 3 = 7$.

**Answer: 7**

cemc-fryer-2025-02b.title: Points per game
cemc-fryer-2025-02b.body:
A tie contributes 2 to $S$ and a decided game contributes 4. With $t$ ties out of 3 games, $S = 2t + 4(3 - t) = 12 - 2t$. Setting $12 - 2t = 6$ gives $t = 3$.

**Answer: 3 (all games were ties)**

cemc-fryer-2025-02c.title: Equation
cemc-fryer-2025-02c.body:
One tie gives 2 points; two decided games give $2W$. So $2W + 2 = 24$ and $W = 11$.

**Answer: $W = 11$**

cemc-fryer-2025-02c.title: Remove the tie
cemc-fryer-2025-02c.body:
Without the tie's 2 points, $24 - 2 = 22$ points came from two wins, so each win is worth $11$.

**Answer: $W = 11$**

cemc-fryer-2025-02d.title: Case on the number of ties
Divisibility view
cemc-fryer-2025-02d.body:
$21 - 2t$ must be divisible by $3 - t$. For $t = 0, 1, 2$: $21/3 = 7$ ✓, $19/2$ ✗, $17/1 = 17$ ✓; $t = 3$ leaves no decided games and $S = 6$. Both values are achievable (e.g. every game decided with $W = 7$; two ties and one decided game with $W = 17$).

**Answer: $W = 7$ or $17$**

cemc-fryer-2025-03a.title: Even exponents
cemc-fryer-2025-03a.body:
A number is a perfect square exactly when every prime in its factorization has an even exponent. $2^3 \times 3^2$ has an odd power of 2, so $j$ must have an odd power of 2 and an even power of every other prime: $j = 2 \times (\text{square})$ or $8 \times (\text{square})$, etc.

With $j \le 20$: $2 \times 1 = 2$, $2 \times 4 = 8$, $2 \times 9 = 18$ ($2 \times 16 = 32$ is too big). Note $8 = 2 \times 4$ is already listed.

**Answer: $j = 2, 8, 18$**

cemc-fryer-2025-03a.title: Simplify first
cemc-fryer-2025-03a.body:
$2^3 \times 3^2 \times j = (2 \times 3)^2 \times 2j$, which is a perfect square exactly when $2j$ is. With $2j \le 40$ even and a perfect square: $2j \in \{4, 16, 36\}$, so $j \in \{2, 8, 18\}$.

**Answer: $j = 2, 8, 18$**

cemc-fryer-2025-03b.title: List square divisors of 3600
cemc-fryer-2025-03b.body:
$20k$ must be a perfect square dividing $3600 = 60^2$, so $20k = d^2$ with $d \mid 60$. Also $20 \mid d^2$ requires $2 \mid d$ and $5 \mid d$, i.e. $10 \mid d$. Divisors of 60 that are multiples of 10: $10, 20, 30, 60$, giving $20k = 100, 400, 900, 3600$, so $k = 5, 20, 45, 180$.

**Answer: $k = 5, 20, 45, 180$**

cemc-fryer-2025-03c.title: Count by the value of $ab$
cemc-fryer-2025-03c.body:
$a^2 b^2 = (ab)^2$ must be a square divisor of $2025 = 3^4 \cdot 5^2$; then $c$ is determined. So $ab$ must be a divisor of $45 = 3^2 \cdot 5$, and for each such $m = ab$ we count the ordered factorizations $m = a \cdot b$, which is the number of divisors of $m$.

| $m = ab$ | 1 | 3 | 5 | 9 | 15 | 45 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| divisors of $m$ | 1 | 2 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 6 |

Total $1 + 2 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 6 = 18$.

**Answer: 18**

cemc-fryer-2025-03c.title: Exponents of 3 and 5 separately
cemc-fryer-2025-03c.body:
Write $a = 3^{a_1}5^{a_2}$, $b = 3^{b_1}5^{b_2}$, $c = 3^{c_1}5^{c_2}$. We need $2a_1 + 2b_1 + c_1 = 4$ and $2a_2 + 2b_2 + c_2 = 2$ with non-negative integers.

- For 3: $a_1 + b_1 \in \{0, 1, 2\}$ (then $c_1 = 4 - 2(a_1 + b_1)$), giving $1 + 2 + 3 = 6$ choices.
- For 5: $a_2 + b_2 \in \{0, 1\}$, giving $1 + 2 = 3$ choices.

Total $6 \times 3 = 18$.

**Answer: 18**

cemc-fryer-2025-04a.title: Same base, same height
cemc-fryer-2025-04a.body:
Each triangle has base $AB = 7$ on the $x$-axis and third vertex on the line $y = 4$, so each has height 4 and area $\frac12 \cdot 7 \cdot 4 = 14$. Sum: $3 \times 14 = 42$.

**Answer: 42**

cemc-fryer-2025-04a.title: Half the parallelogram
cemc-fryer-2025-04a.body:
The parallelogram has area $7 \times 4 = 28$. Each of the three triangles has base $AB$ and apex on the opposite side, so it has half the parallelogram's area, 14. Sum: 42.

**Answer: 42**

cemc-fryer-2025-04b.title: Count lattice points on each side
cemc-fryer-2025-04b.body:
$G$ cannot be on line $CD$ (the triangle would be flat). Lattice points on $AB$: $(0,0), \ldots, (7, 0)$ — 8 points. On $AD$ (from $(0,0)$ to $(2,4)$) the only new one is $(1, 2)$; on $BC$ (from $(7,0)$ to $(9,4)$) the only new one is $(8, 2)$. Total $8 + 1 + 1 = 10$.

**Answer: 10**

cemc-fryer-2025-04b.title: Count all, then remove
cemc-fryer-2025-04b.body:
The perimeter contains $8$ lattice points on $AB$, $8$ on $CD$, and $(1, 2)$, $(8, 2)$ in between: 18 in total. Removing the 8 on $CD$ leaves $10$.

**Answer: 10**

cemc-fryer-2025-04c.title: Organize by where the vertices lie
cemc-fryer-2025-04c.body:
The 18 lattice points on the perimeter are 8 on $AB$ ($y = 0$), 8 on $CD$ ($y = 4$), and $M(1, 2)$, $N(8, 2)$. Segments on $AB$ (or on $CD$) with lattice endpoints: length $L$ occurs $8 - L$ times, so the sum of their lengths is $\sum_{L=1}^{7} L(8-L) = 84$. Note $MN = 7$.

- **Two vertices on $AB$, one on $CD$** (height 4): $8 \cdot \frac12 \cdot 4 \cdot 84 = 1344$; same for two on $CD$ and one on $AB$: total $2688$.
- **Two on $AB$ (or $CD$), one at $M$ or $N$** (height 2): $2 \cdot \frac12 \cdot 2 \cdot 84 = 168$ for each long side: total $336$.
- **One on $AB$ ($P$), one on $CD$ ($Q$), one of $M, N$:** $[PMQ] + [PNQ] = [PMN] + [QMN]$ (the segment $MN$ at height 2 splits the quadrilateral $PMQN$ two ways), and $[PMN] = [QMN] = \frac12 \cdot 7 \cdot 2 = 7$. So each of the $64$ pairs $(P, Q)$ contributes 14: total $896$.
- **$M$, $N$ and one other point** (height 2 over base 7): $16 \cdot 7 = 112$.

(Triples on one line — three on $AB$, three on $CD$ — have zero area and don't matter.)

Sum: $2688 + 336 + 896 + 112 = 4032$.

**Answer: 4032**

cemc-fryer-2025-04c.title: Sum by pairs of horizontal levels
cemc-fryer-2025-04c.body:
Use the shoelace idea through heights: all points lie on the three horizontal lines $y = 0$, $y = 2$, $y = 4$.

- Two points on one line and the third on another: area $= \frac12 \cdot (\text{base}) \cdot (\text{height difference})$. Bases on $y = 0$ or $y = 4$ sum to 84 (as in the first solution); on $y = 2$ there is one base, $MN = 7$.
  - Base on $y=0$, apex on $y=4$ (8 apexes, height 4): $8 \cdot 2 \cdot 84 = 1344$; base on $y=4$, apex on $y = 0$: 1344.
  - Base on $y = 0$ or $y = 4$, apex $M$ or $N$ (height 2): $2 \cdot 2 \cdot 1 \cdot 84 = 336$.
  - Base $MN$, apex on $y = 0$ or $y = 4$ (16 apexes, height 2): $16 \cdot 7 = 112$.
- One point on each line, $P = (p, 0)$, $X \in \{M, N\}$, $Q = (q, 4)$: the midpoint $K$ of $PQ$ is $\left(\frac{p+q}{2}, 2\right)$, on the line $y = 2$. The horizontal segment $XK$ splits $\triangle PXQ$ into two triangles with base $XK$ and height 2 each, so $[PXQ] = 2 \cdot XK$. Since $0 \le p \le 7$ and $2 \le q \le 9$, $K$ lies between $M$ ($x = 1$) and $N$ ($x = 8$), so $KM + KN = 7$ and each pair $(P, Q)$ contributes $2 \cdot 7 = 14$: $64 \cdot 14 = 896$.

Sum: $1344 + 1344 + 336 + 112 + 896 = 4032$.

**Answer: 4032**
